The flaw resides in the XSRF token protection logic, where the withXSRFToken config property is evaluated using JavaScript truthy/falsy semantics instead of strict boolean comparison. This allows an attacker, via prototype pollution or misconfiguration, to set withXSRFToken to a truthy non-boolean value (e.g., an object or string), which short-circuits the same-origin check (isURLSameOrigin). Consequently, XSRF tokens are sent to all request targets, including cross-origin servers controlled by an attacker, enabling potential CSRF attacks. The vulnerability is rated with a CVSS score of 5.4 (Medium) and has a very low EPSS score (0.0%), indicating low exploitation likelihood in the wild. Patches are available in Axios versions 1.15.1 and 0.31.1. Supply Chain & Package Security Axios is a widely used npm package with millions of weekly downloads. This vulnerability highlights the risk of prototype pollution in JavaScript libraries, which can be exploited to bypass security controls. Organizations using Axios in their supply chain should immediately update to the patched versions to prevent potential CSRF attacks. The vulnerability does not affect the integrity of the package itself but rather its runtime behavior when misconfigured. Basic Information for CVE-2026-42042 Vulnerability Information Axios: XSRF Token Cross-Origin Leakage via Prototype Pollution Gadget in withXSRFToken Boolean Coercion Overview In versions of Axios prior to 1.15.1 (browser-side) and 0.31.1 (Node.js-side), the withXSRFToken configuration option is evaluated using JavaScript’s truthy/falsy semantics instead of strict boolean comparison. This causes the same-origin check to be skipped when the value is a truthy non-boolean type, resulting in the XSRF token being sent to any request target—including attacker-controlled cross-origin servers. Affected Versions Axios < 1.15.1 (browser-side) Axios < 0.31.1 (Node.js-side) Details The XSRF protection logic relies on withXSRFToken to determine whether to attach the token. The code uses truthy/falsy semantics for this configuration, rather than strict === true/false. When withXSRFToken is set to any truthy non-boolean type (e.g., via prototype pollution or misconfiguration), the same-origin check (isURLSameOrigin) is short-circuited. Result: The XSRF token is sent with requests to all targets, including cross-origin servers controlled by an attacker. Impact An attacker can induce the client to send requests containing the XSRF token to a malicious cross-origin server, bypassing same-origin restrictions, which may lead to successful cross-site request forgery attacks.
